Findings.Comment: The guard now sets `last` to `len(lines) + 1` when the context window reaches or exceeds the end of the file. Go slice expressions panic when the upper bound exceeds `len(s)`. For example, given a 10-element slice where `first = 7` and `n = 4`, `last` becomes 11, `last >= 10` triggers, `last` is set to 11, and `lines[7:11]` panics with "slice bounds out of range". The old `if last > len(lines) { last = len(lines) }` was correct.
Findings.Headline: ContextAfter panics when context reaches end of file — off-by-one

Expected.why: The clamp sets last to len(lines)+1, so the final slice expression lines[first:last] runs one past the length. With no spare capacity that panics; with spare capacity it silently yields a phantom trailing line, which is the quieter half of the bug.

Findings.Comment: This condition causes an out-of-bounds panic when slicing the `lines` slice. If `first` is 0 and `n` is 0, `first` equals `last` and the function returns `nil` correctly. However, when `first` is a valid index and `last` is set to `len(lines) + 1`, the slice expression `lines[first:last]` will attempt to access `lines[len(lines)]`, which is one past the last valid index (since Go slices are zero-indexed). For example, with a 3-element slice, `len(lines) + 1` is 4, and `lines[0:4]` panics. The correct behavior is to cap at `len(lines)`.
Findings.Headline: Off-by-one causes slice out-of-bounds panic

Expected.why: The clamp sets last to len(lines)+1, so the final slice expression lines[first:last] runs one past the length. With no spare capacity that panics; with spare capacity it silently yields a phantom trailing line, which is the quieter half of the bug.

Findings.Comment: Setting `last` to `len(lines) + 1` creates an out-of-bounds slice. `lines` has valid indices 0 through `len(lines)-1`. When `first` is less than `len(lines)` and `last` is set to `len(lines)+1`, the slice `lines[first:last]` will panic at runtime because `last` exceeds the slice's capacity. Example: if `first=0` and `len(lines)=5`, `last` becomes 6, causing `lines[0:6]` to panic.

Findings.Comment: The condition change from `last > len(lines)` to `last >= len(lines)` combined with setting `last = len(lines) + 1` introduces an off-by-one error. When `first + n` equals the length of `lines` (e.g., `first` is 7 and `n` is 3 with 10 lines), the new code sets `last` to 11, which is one past the end of the slice. Since `first` (7) is less than `last` (11), the slice `lines[7:11]` is attempted, causing a runtime panic due to index out of range. Findings.Comment: The `defer resp.Body.Close()` was removed, but the function reads `resp.Body` via `json.Decode` and never closes it. Per Go's net/http documentation, the caller must close `resp.Body` when done reading. If an early return occurs (e.g., non-2xx status), the body is never closed, leaking the underlying TCP connection and associated resources until the client's idle timeout expires. Under high concurrency, this can exhaust file descriptors or connection pools.

Findings.Comment: The error returned by `tx.Commit(ctx)` is ignored. If the commit fails (e.g., due to a constraint violation or connection issue), the function returns nil, indicating success to the caller even though the transaction was not persisted. This can cause silent data loss or inconsistent state where the caller believes the claim was added when it was not. The deferred `tx.Rollback` will not trigger on a successful return, leaving the failed transaction to be cleaned up later without error propagation.

This leads to silent data loss where a user is told a claim succeeded when it did not.

Findings.Comment: The error sentinels in the two error-handling branches have been swapped, breaking the contract documented by `ErrNoClaim`. Now, when a database query returns no rows, the error wraps `errNoRows` (an unexported error) instead of `ErrNoClaim`, and any other database error wraps `ErrNoClaim` instead of the actual error. This means callers who check `errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim)` will incorrectly treat a database fault as a 'no claim' condition and will fail to detect an actual missing claim.
Findings.Headline: Swapped error sentinels break ErrNoClaim contract — blocking

Expected.why: The branches wrap each other's error: errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim) is now false when the project is genuinely unclaimed and true when the query failed, so a database fault is treated as an unowned project.

Findings.Comment: The `Owner` function is meant to return `ErrNoClaim` when no rows are found and a wrapped original error for any other database fault. The diff swaps these: it now wraps `err` (which is `errNoRows`) in the no-rows case and wraps `ErrNoClaim` in the general error case. This inverts the intended contract—callers using `errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim)` will incorrectly get `ErrNoClaim` for database faults and miss it when there is no claim, breaking the "distinguish 'nobody owns it' from a database fault" behavior documented in the function comment.
